messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Prison Guard
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Layla's Vigil

Layla Mansour had worked the night shift at the state correctional facility for twenty-three years without incident. She knew the rhythm of the place—the clang of gates, the predictable patterns of movement through the tiers, the particular silence that fell between count time and lights-out. On a Tuesday evening in March, that knowledge failed her.

She was conducting a routine check of C-block when an inmate she had supervised for five years—a man she had spoken to hundreds of times, whom she believed she understood—lunged at her from a blind spot near the supply closet. His arm came around her neck. For the first seconds, Layla's mind could not catch up to what her body already knew: she was being strangled. Her hands clawed at his forearm. She heard herself making sounds she did not recognize. Another guard pulled him off, but those few seconds had reorganized something fundamental in how Layla moved through the world.

In the weeks after, she returned to work because she had always returned to work. But the facility had become a place of constant calculation. She began arriving earlier to walk the blocks before the inmates were released for breakfast, her eyes moving systematically across every corner, every shadow, every potential hiding place. She positioned herself with her back always to a wall. During her shifts, she found herself unable to stand still—she would pace the tiers, check the same supply closet repeatedly, scan faces for signs of aggression she might have missed before. Her supervisor eventually asked if she was well. She said yes.

At home, sleep became something that happened to other people. She would lie beside her husband Reza, her body tense, waiting for danger that did not come. When she did drift off, she would jolt awake at small sounds—the refrigerator humming, a car passing on the street. Reza would reach for her in the dark, and she would flinch. The silence of their house in the early morning hours felt pregnant with threat. She had come to believe that quiet meant something terrible was gathering, that danger announced itself only in the moment before it struck.

What troubled Layla most was not the hypervigilance or the sleeplessness, but the weight of what she had not done. She had been responsible for the safety of everyone in that block—the inmates, yes, but also the younger guards, the nurses who came through during medical rounds. When that inmate attacked her, she had been overcome in seconds. She had not protected anyone. She had barely protected herself. The thought circled endlessly: she should have seen it coming. She should have been better. The fact that she had been supervising that block for years, that she knew its rhythms, made the failure feel absolute. She was supposed to be the one who understood. She was supposed to be the one who kept people safe.

Layla began declining invitations from other guards to grab coffee after shifts. Instead, she would text Reza constantly, asking him to call her, to talk to her, to keep her mind occupied with anything other than her own thoughts. She filled her evenings with noise—the television running, music playing, conversations with Reza that she initiated and sustained through sheer force of will. When he suggested she might want to sit quietly with a book, she felt panic rise in her chest. Alone with her thoughts meant the images would come: the supply closet, the arm around her neck, the knowledge that she had failed.

She began calling in to work more frequently, citing minor illnesses. When she did go in, she found herself avoiding C-block entirely, asking to be reassigned to administrative tasks. Her supervisor noticed. The work she had built her identity around for more than two decades was becoming something she could not bear. She was sixty-eight years old. She had planned to work another five years. Now she was certain that everyone at the facility saw her differently—as the guard who had been overpowered, who had not protected them, who could not be trusted to do her job.

It was Reza who finally said it plainly: something had broken in her, and she needed help. Layla had resisted, but the constant socializing, the dropped responsibilities, the way she now examined every face around her for signs of deception—it was exhausting. She was exhausted. She came to the first appointment afraid that a therapist would confirm what she already believed: that she was permanently changed, that people could not be trusted, that she had become someone she no longer recognized.
